HCI1.title: Introduction to Human-Computer Interaction
HCI1.summary: A comprehensive overview of Human-Computer Interaction (HCI), covering its definition, multidisciplinary nature, importance to usability, and core design principles.
HCI1.content:
What is HCI?

Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) refers to the study and design of the interaction between people (users) and computers. It focuses on creating user-friendly interfaces and experiences. It is a multidisciplinary field that involves:

  • Engineering – creating efficient systems and interfaces.
  • Psychology – understanding user behavior and cognition.
  • Design – making systems attractive and usable.
  • Ergonomics – fitting the system to the human body and needs.

HCI is about designing systems that allow people to interact with technology easily, efficiently, and safely.

Why is it important?

HCI is about doing things better.

  • USABILITY: Resulting interface are easy to use, efficient for the task, ensure safety and to correct completion of the task.

Principles of HCI

  • 1. “Know Thy User”
  • 2. Understand the Task
  • 3. Reduce Memory Load
  • 4. Strive for Consistency
  • 5. Remind Users and Refresh Their Memory
  • 6. Prevent Errors/Reversal of Action
  • 7. Naturalness

Detailed Breakdown of Principles

1. “Know Thy User”

Factors to Consider:

  • Age
  • Gender
  • Education Level
  • Social Status
  • Background in Technology

2. “Understand the Task”

Design should match the steps and logic of the task the user wants to perform.

3. Reduce Memory Load

Users should not be required to memorize (or recall out of their heads) a great deal of information to carry out tasks.

4. Strive for Consistency

Users should not have to wonder whether different words, situations, or actions mean the same thing. Don’t confuse your user. In other words, use all elements across your application consistently.

5. Remind Users and Refresh Their Memory

Any significant task will involve the use of memory, so another good strategy is to employ interfaces that give continuous reminders of important information and thereby refresh the user’s memory.

6. Prevent Errors/Reversal of Action

Users hate errors, and even more so hate the feeling that they themselves have done something wrong. Either eliminate error-prone conditions or check for them and notify users about that before they commit to the action.

Error Prevention:

  • Error prevention over error correction.
  • Automatic detection of errors.
  • Clear error notifications.
  • Offer solutions for problems.

7. Naturalness

The final major HCI principle is to favor “natural” interaction and interfaces.

  • Follows from the free choice of modalities and may result in a human-computer interaction that is close to human-human communication.

Conclusion

Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) plays a vital role in making technology easier, more effective, and more enjoyable to use. The principles of HCI guide us in designing interfaces that are not only visually appealing but also user-centered and efficient. As future designers and developers, we must always prioritize the user experience in everything we create.

HCI2.title: Guidelines Categories and Example Guidelines
HCI2.summary: An in-depth exploration of specific, task-based, user-group focused, and platform-dependent rules for interface design, including categories, 9 general design guidelines, and application challenges.
HCI2.content:
Characteristics of HCI Guidelines

HCI guidelines are more specific than general principles and are often:

  • Task-based
  • User-group focused
  • Platform-dependent

Types of Guidelines (Categories)

Guidelines are categorized to address different design contexts:

  • User Type: Examples include kids, the elderly, and people with disabilities.
  • Platform/System: Examples include mobile, desktop, embedded systems, and public kiosks.
  • Vendor/Brand: Examples include iOS, Android, Windows, and company branding.
  • Interaction Style: Examples include GUI, voice input, gesture, touchscreen, and haptics.
  • Task Context: Examples include driving, shopping, outdoor use, and eyes-free scenarios.
  • Application Type: Examples include games, e-commerce, social media, and navigation.

9 General HCI Design Guidelines

1. Visual Display Layout

Focuses on how to arrange elements on the screen:

  • Avoid clutter.
  • Use alignment and whitespace.
  • Highlight key content at the top or center.
  • Use consistent formatting.

Example: U.S. government website design recommends placing clickable buttons near the top and center for easy access.

2. Information Structuring & Navigation

Focuses on how users move and access info:

  • Organize content logically, either hierarchically or sequentially.
  • Use navigation aids like breadcrumbs, tabs, menus, sidebars, site maps, and search features.

Key Patterns:

  • Two-Panel Selector: A list is on the left while details are on the right.
  • One-Window Drilldown: Tapping to move forward or back, typical in mobile apps.

3. Taking User Input

Defined as "Efficient and accurate input methods":

  • Use drop-downs, radio buttons, and checkboxes.
  • Use auto-complete or suggested values.
  • Minimize typing to reduce errors.
  • Use default values.
  • Avoid placing conflicting buttons (e.g., “Submit” and “Cancel”) too close together.

Example: A calendar form with structured dropdowns for day, month, and year reduces user error.

4. Design for Users with Disabilities

Based on Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG 2.0):

  • Provide text alternatives for images.
  • Allow keyboard-only navigation.
  • Avoid flashing content to prevent seizure risks.
  • Use captions for video and audio.
  • Make color and contrast adjustable.

5. Design for Mobile Devices

Addresses constraints like small screens, varying orientations, and touch input:

  • Minimize typing.
  • Use larger, thumb-friendly touch areas.
  • Optimize screen space using scrollable panels or tabs.
  • Keep users focused with clear paths.

6. Vendor-Specific Styles

Following official company interface guidelines:

  • Apple iOS: Icons have consistent shapes, resolution standards, and are auto-styled with rounded corners and shine effects.
  • Microsoft Windows XP Fonts: Uses Trebuchet for titles and Tahoma for body text.

7. Aural Interfaces (Earcons)

Sound-based cues categorized by their relationship to the action:

  • Symbolic: Abstract sounds, like applause for success.
  • Nomic: Real-world sounds, such as a door slam.
  • Metaphoric: Sounds that represent an action, like a rising pitch for an upload.

8. Designing for Driving or Hands-Free Tasks

For car interfaces or voice systems:

  • Use voice commands that match on-screen buttons.
  • Group related buttons together.
  • Avoid distracting visuals or complex steps.

9. E-Commerce UI Design

Guidelines for online shopping:

  • Must be linear and guided (e.g., cart → shipping → payment → confirmation).
  • Provide feedback at each stage.
  • Separate billing and shipping steps.
  • Include options for guest checkout.

Challenges in Applying Guidelines

  • Volume: Too many guidelines can make them hard to prioritize.
  • Conflicts: Brand colors may conflict with accessibility requirements.
  • Constraints: Time and resources may be limited.
  • Technology Gap: New technology like AR/VR may lack mature guidelines.

Design Tip: Experienced designers must balance these trade-offs and follow the most critical guidelines based on the specific user, task, and platform.
